children.html: Beyond g and c: The Relationship of Rated Creativity to Long-Term Storage and Retrieval (Glr)
Maria J. Avitia and James C. Kaufman University of Connecticut

The relationship between creativity and intelligence has been explored in many ways, including using the CHC theory's constructs of Fluid Reasoning (Gf) and Crystallized Knowledge (Gc). Yet the primary CHC broad factor theoretically associated with creativity is considered to be Long-term storage and retrieval (Glr). To test the relationship between Glr and creativity, 116 participants were tested on 4 Glr subtests from the Kaufman Assessment Battery for Children–II (Kaufman & Kaufman, 2004), a Gc subtest from the Kaufman Test of Educational Achievement – II Brief (Kaufman & Kaufman, 2005), and multiple creativity measures including self-assessments and rated creative performance in drawing and writing. Glr was significantly related to creative drawing, but not creative writing or most self-assessed creativity measures.
Keywords: assessment, Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) theory, creativity, Glr, intelligence

The relationship between creativity and intelligence was one of the early questions to be studied in creativity research (e.g., Barron, 1963; Getzels & Jackson, 1962; Wallach & Kohan, 1965) and continues to be a hot topic today (J. C. Kaufman & Plucker, 2011; Kim, Cramond, & VanTassel-Baska, 2010). Most work, however, assumes a connection; as Plucker and Renzulli (1999) concluded, it is now a matter of uncovering not whether but how the two are related.

Both intelligence and creativity are nuanced constructs that are time-consuming to assess well. Most studies, for example, use divergent thinking tests to measure creativity and group-based tests of g (or general intelligence) to measure intelligence (see Barron & Harrington, 1981, and Kim, 2005 for an overview of many studies). Using these types of measures, creativity and intelligence are moderately correlated. Kim (2005) conducted an extensive meta-analysis of 21 studies containing 45,000 participants and using multiple measures of IQ and creativity. She found very small positive correlations (mean correlation of .174) between measures of cognitive ability (designed to measure g) and measures of creativity (primarily divergent thinking).
Although Group IQ tests serve a strong purpose in research studies, they are not used by most school psychologists for psychoeducational assessment (A. S. Kaufman & Lichtenberger,

2006). In addition, most current IQ tests use the Cattell-Horn-Carroll (CHC) model (A. S. Kaufman, 2009) either explicitly or implicitly in their theoretical framework (Keith & Reynolds, 2010), in addition to producing an overall g score.

The CHC model is derived from the Cattell-Horn Gf–Gc theory of fluid and crystallized intelligence (Horn & Cattell, 1966) and Carroll's (1993) Three-Stratum Theory. Both the Cattell-Horn and Carroll models essentially started from the same point—Spearman's (1904) g-factor theory; though they took different paths, they ended up with remarkably consistent conclusions about the spectrum of broad cognitive abilities. Horn and Cattell built upon Spearman's g to posit two kinds of g: Fluid intelligence (Gf), the ability to apply a variety of mental operations to solve novel problems, ones that don't benefit from past learning or experience, and Crystallized intelligence (Gc), the breadth and depth of a person's accumulated knowledge of a culture and the ability to use that knowledge to solve problems (Horn & Cattell, 1966). Horn subsequently revised and expanded Gf–Gc theory to incorporate 8 –10 broad abilities, including Gf and Gc and other abilities such as Short-term Memory (Gsm), Visual Processing (Gv), Processing Speed (Gs), and Long-Term Retrieval (Glr; see, e.g., Horn & Blankson, 2005; Horn & Hofer, 1992; Horn & Noll, 1997).

Creativity was hypothesized to be strongly linked to Gf in the early stages of the Cattell-Horn Gf-Gc theory (Cattell & Butcher, 1968). However, such a relationship is no longer explicitly part of the CHC theory. Creativity is primarily related to Long term storage and retrieval (Glr), the ability to store information in and fluently retrieve new or previously acquired information (e.g., concepts, ideas, items, names) from long-term memory (Flanagan, Ortiz, & Alfonso, 2007).

In current CHC theory, Glr has two distinct components: learning efficiency (the ability to learn and retain new information) and fluency (e.g., the ability to name as many "things" as possible in 30 seconds). These components each have multiple "narrow abilities"

that are specific skills related to the broader constructs. One such narrow ability is Idea Production (also known as retrieval fluency), which emphasizes a person's efficiency at retrieving information from long-term memory. Idea Production is the set of abilities (e.g., fluency, flexibility, originality) that has long been associated with creativity (Schneider & McGrew, 2012), most notably Guilford's (1967) operation of Divergent Production.

As mentioned above, "Some Glr narrow abilities have been prominent in creativity research (e.g., production, ideational fluency, or associative fluency)" (McGrew, 2009, p. 6). In a detailed description of the model, this sentence is the only mention of creativity, originality, or divergent thinking. Fluid intelligence (Gf) is discussed in terms of its relationship to problem-solving and coping with novel problems (both considered to be highly related to creativity). Nonetheless, in current discussions of the relationship of creativity to intelligence as presented by the CHC model, the emphasis is on Glr. Several of the narrow abilities incorporated into Glr, such as Ideational Fluency, Associational Fluency, and (unsurprisingly) Originality/Creativity, have been specifically hypothesized to relate strongly to creativity (J. C. Kaufman, S. B. Kaufman, & Lichtenberger, 2011).

The connection between Glr and creativity is backed by extensive research and theory in creative cognition. Scholars from Wallas (1926) to Finke, Ward, and Smith (1992) discuss cognitive processes that apply preexisting knowledge to new concepts. Mednick's (1962) theory of remote associations posits that the ability to organize and access ideas within memory aided creativity by allowing for more remote associations between ideas (i.e., connecting the concept of "dog" with "cat" is less remote than "dog" with "colorblind" or "dogwood"). His measure, the Remote Associates Test (RAT; Mednick, 1968), is a common test of creative problem solving that requires people to find a word that is associated with three other words (e.g., Sleeping, Bean, and Trash are all connected to the word Bag).

Additional work has studied the link between creativity and memory from a neuropsychological perspective. Gabora (2010), for example, has proposed that analytic thought triggers standard neurons (dog-cat type associations), whereas associative thought activates additional neurons (which she dubs "neurds"). The "neurds" that are activated bring with them the associations most relevant for the specific context. So, for example, the dogcolorblind word association might occur if the word "dog" is used in a visual processing situation (i.e., a context that encourages visualization). The act of engaging in associative thought may bring added cognitive capacity.

Retrieval-induced forgetting is when remembering some information causes related information to be forgotten or inhibits retrieval of the related information (MacLeod & Macrae, 2001). Bristol and Viskontas (2006) connect this concept with the notion of creativity occurring with reduced cortical inhibition; they argue that people who are less prone to such retrieval-induced forgetting will also be more creative. Interestingly, Storm, Angello, and Bjork (2011) found that when people take the Remote Associates Test they are more likely to forget other common associated words. This tendency, called goal-directed forgetting (Bjork, Bjork, & Anderson, 1998), is linked to better creative problem solving. The relationship between memory and creativity is not a simple positive association, consistent with Glr's emphasis on being able to retrieve the best response from storage.

Despite the theoretical relationship between Glr and creativity, most imperial work has focused instead Gf and Gc. For example, Sligh, Connors, and Roskos-Ewoldsen (2005) found that Gc was significantly correlated with creativity in people of average intelligence, whereas Gf was significantly correlated with creativity in people of high intelligence. This study is but one of many to explore the often contradictory relationships between Gf, Gc, and creativity (see, Batey, Chamorro-Premuzic, & Furnham, 2009; Furnham & Chamorro-Premuzic, 2006; Nusbaum & Silvia, 2011).

In contrast, there is a striking lack of research on how creativity is empirically connected to Glr. Silvia, Beaty, and Nusbaum (2013), in one of the few studies to do so, examined how divergent thinking performance related to multiple verbal fluency tests (representing the lower order Glr factors related to fluency). Silvia et al. found that the primary Glr factor had a significant effect on both the creativity (originality) of divergent thinking performance (- .443, p .001) and the fluency (- .399, p .001). In a similar vein, Benedek, Könen, and Neubauer (2012) used cognitive tasks that are comparable to Glr, such as associative fluency, and also found strong relationships with divergent thinking measures. These studies are a good starting point, but more work is needed.

As mentioned earlier, most studies of creativity and intelligence use g. In addition, however, they also tend to use general measures of creativity (what could be called c). These measures (such as divergent thinking or the RAT) tend to produce an overall creativity score comparable with g. Another point of view is that of domain specificity—that creativity has subcomponents similar to intelligence (such as everyday creativity, performance, or art; J. C. Kaufman, 2012). Just as in the intelligence research literature there is an active debate between people who espouse g and those who argue for different models (whether CHC or multiple intelligences), so too is there a comparable debate in the creativity literature over c (see J. C. Kaufman, 2009, for a detailed discussion).

Most current discussions of creativity assessment argue that at the very least, the question of domain specificity should be considered (J. C. Kaufman, Plucker, & Baer, 2008). Most studies of creative performance in multiple domains do not find high correlations (e.g., Baer, 1991, 1993; Han, 2003; J. C. Kaufman, Evans, & Baer, 2010). A recent factor analysis of self-reported creativity found that a domain-specific solution was a better fit than a single-factor solution (J. C. Kaufman, Cole, & Baer, 2009). Therefore, an additional new component of this study will be to use multiple measures of domain-specific creativity.

In the present study, the measures of Glr are measures of learning efficiency, not fluency. Whether or not these tests of Glr are hypothesized to correlate significantly with ratings of an individual's creativity in poetry and drawing depends upon one's theoretical orientation. From Carroll's (1993) original theory, Memory & Learning and Idea Production were identified as separate constructs. Therefore, from that perspective, one would hypothesize no significant correlation between measures of learning efficiency and creativity ratings. By contrast, contemporary CHC theory posits that learning efficiency and retrieval fluency are aspects of the same construct (Schneider & McGrew, 2012). Thus, measures of learning ability should correlate positively with any measure of creativity that requires novel combinations and conceptual integration (Rothenberg, 1988). Both traditional measures
of creativity (such as the RAT) and actual creative performance require these underlying cognitive processes (Finke et al., 1992).

In accordance with CHC theory, we hypothesize that creativity (as measured with two performance assessments, an achievement questionnaire, and a self-report measure) will account for more variance in Glr than in Gc (H1). In addition, based on the domain specific approach to creativity, we hypothesize that rated creative performance in two distinct domains (art and writing) will show significantly different relationships with the measures of intelligence (H2).

Participants consisted of 116 (33 male, 83 female) students attending a large public university in Southern California. Ages ranged from 18 to 58 with a mean age of 26 years. Of the participants, ethnicity was reported as follows: 19 African American, 9 Asian American, 29 European American, 47 Hispanic American, 1 Native American, 2 Middle Eastern, and 9 biracial. Participants were offered extra credit for participating in the study.

Intelligence measures. Long term storage and retrieval (Glr) was measured with four subtests from the Kaufman Assessment Battery for Children–Second Edition (KABC-II; A. S. Kaufman & N. L. Kaufman, 2004): Atlantis, Rebus, Atlantis Delayed, and Rebus Delayed. Although the Kaufman Adult Intelligence Test (KAIT; A. S. Kaufman & N. L. Kaufman, 1993) includes a measure of Glr, the authors decided to use the KABC-II for this study because it provides more measures of Glr by including Atlantis and Atlantis Delayed. Even though the sample was older than the normed group, the scaled scores used in this study were calculated from preexisting norms that were presented in the KABC-II Manual (see Table D.1, for the 18:6 –18:11 age group, p. 172). The age difference in the normed group and the sample did not present an issue because the scores were only used for correlations within the sample and not a direct measure of the Participants Long-Term storage and Retrieval abilities.

Atlantis. In this subtest, the participant is taught nonsense names for pictures of fish, plants, and shells. The participant demonstrates learning by selecting, from an array of pictures, the specific picture named by the examiner. Items are scored 2–1– 0; 2 points for a correct response and 1 point for a correct category (e.g., pointing to a fish, but the wrong fish). There are 54 items and scores can range from 0 –108.

Rebus. The participant is taught words or concepts that are associated with rebuses (drawings), then "reads" aloud the phrases and sentences that are composed of these rebuses. There are 21 items and scores can range from 0 to 78. Depending on how many items correct, the participant earns partial or full credit.

Atlantis Delayed. The participant demonstrates delayed recall of paired associations learned about 15–25 minutes earlier during the Atlantis subtest by pointing to the picture named by the examiner. Items are scored for pointing at the right picture (2 points) or pointing to the right category (1 point). There are 12 items and scores can range from 0 to 24.

Rebus Delayed. The participant demonstrates delayed recall of the previously learned rebuses 15–25 minutes after they are taught by reading phrases and sentences composed of the same rebuses. There are 11 items and scores can range from 0 to 47.

The raw scores for the four Glr subtests were converted to scaled scores using a linear transformation with a mean of 10 and an SD of 3 (A. S. Kaufman & N. L. Kaufman, 2004). Even though we had an adult sample, we used scaled scores versus raw scores because scaled scores were needed to derive the overall Glr score. Although these scores do not reflect participants' actual Glr ability as mentioned above, it allows us to understand the degree to which the participants' overall Glr ability was related to the quality of their creative products. The overall Glr score was computed by tabulating the mean for both the Glr Immediate Learning standard score and that of the Glr Delayed Recall standard score.

The Glr Immediate Learning standard score was computed by summing the scaled scores for the Atlantis and Rebus subtests and then converting it to a standard score based on tables provided in the KABC-II Manual (A. S. Kaufman & N. L. Kaufman, 2004). The Glr Delayed Recall standard score was computed in the same manner, using Atlantis Delayed and Rebus Delayed. Standard Scores are based on a mean of 100 and an SD of 15.

Gc was measured using the Reading subtest from the Kaufman Test of Educational Achievement—Second Edition Brief Form (KTEA-II; A. S. Kaufman & N. L. Kaufman, 2005). Although reading subtest are traditionally thought to measure Grw which is correlated to Gc, a study by S. B. Kaufman, Reynolds, Liu, A. S. Kaufman, and McGrew (2012) on Cognitive–g and Academic–g found that not only are reading subtests correlated to Gc but they are valid measures of Gc as well as Grw. Furthermore, as Hebben and Milberg (2009) state, "skills such as word reading are highly correlated with intelligence and are often the best means for estimating premorbid mental ability" (p. 101)—in other words, reading tests are often used as proxies for an adult's Gc to estimate intelligence before the onset of brain damage.

Reading. This test is comprises two parts. The first part is word recognition, where the participants read words of increasing difficulty that do not follow phonetic rules. There are 46 items scored 0 –1. The second part is reading comprehension. There are 27 items, scored 0 –1, that measure understanding of the material that is read. Total scores can range from 0 –73. Raw scores are converted to standard scores (M 100, SD 15) for the total Reading score. This subtest is included in the KTEA-II Brief Form (A. S. Kaufman & N. L. Kaufman, 2005).
Creativity measures. Creativity was measured using two creative performance tasks rated using the Consensual Assessment Technique, self-reported creative accomplishments, and a brief self-assessment.

Consensual Assessment Technique (CAT; Amabile, 1996). Two actual measures of creative performance were used: writing a poem and drawing a picture. Consistent with past assessments of creativity performance (Amabile, 1996), the participants were given as much time as they needed to finish the task. If participants asked for direction they were told to draw and or write whatever came to mind. The prompt for the poem was Write a poem on the topic of "An embarrassing moment." The prompt for the drawing was, Draw a picture of something that makes you happy.
The CAT has used across many different prompts, with strong reliability across raters being found across multiple domains, in-

cluding visual art (Amabile, 1996; Hennessey, Kim, Guomin, & Weiwei, 2008), creative writing (Baer, Kaufman, & Gentile, 2004; Baer, Kaufman, & Riggs, 2009), mathematical equations (Baer, 1993), photo captions (J. C. Kaufman, Lee, Baer, & Lee, 2007), photographic essays (Dollinger, 2007), designs (Haller, Courvoisier, & Cropley, 2010), dramatic performance (Myford, 1989), music compositions (Hickey, 2001; Priest, 2006), scientific thinking (J. C. Kaufman et al., 2010), and mousetrap inventions (J. C. Kaufman, Baer, Cropley, Reiter-Palmon, & Sinnett, 2013).

The two tasks were scored for creativity by raters based on their own personal definition of creativity; no additional guidance, descriptors, or material on creativity were provided. Raters did not meet or talk about their scores with one another or with the experimenters. This format is consistent with Amabile's (1996) CAT method. Raters assigned scores on a Likert scale from 1 (not at all creative) to 6 (extremely creative).

Although raters should ideally be an expert in a domain (J. C. Kaufman & Baer, 2012), quasi-experts (i.e., people with a certain degree of expertise in a domain) have shown solid reliability correspond reasonably with experts (J. C. Kaufman et al., 2013; J. C. Kaufman, Gentile, & Baer, 2005; Plucker, Kaufman, Temple, & Qian, 2009). For this study, the raters were nine honors and master psychology students who had received formal instruction in creativity and had participated in research on this topic. These students would be considered "quasi experts" based on the definitions posed by J. C. Kaufman and Baer (2012).

Creative Achievement Questionnaire (CAQ; Carson, Peterson, & Higgins, 2005). The CAQ is a measure of creative accomplishments. Participants are presented with levels of creative achievement in 10 domains: visual arts, music, dance, architectural design, creative writing, humor, inventions, scientific discovery, theater/film, and culinary arts. Participant creative achievement is measured by their response to eight statements that participants can endorse that emphasize concrete and public accomplishments (e.g., I have had a showing of my work in a gallery); it is designed so that the more public and national recognition one has, the higher the weight of the scores. Thus, although responses are binary (yes or no), each additional statement is assigned a higher weight, so that I play one or more musical instruments proficiently is scored as one point and My compositions have been critiqued in a national publication is scored as seven points. This also ensures fewer people check statements at the higher ranges.

Participant scores for each domain were recorded by adding all the endorsements for that category based on the weight of each question. The scores can range from 0 (having no training or talent in the area) to 28 (selecting all categories all the way up to my work has been recognized nationally). Most participants would tend to receive lower scores (Silvia, Wigert, Reiter-Palmon, & Kaufman, 2012). Test–retest reliability in a group of college students was r .81 (p .0001), and predictive validity was r .59 (Carson et al., 2005).

Self-assessment of creativity (SAC; adapted from J. C. Kaufman & Baer, 2004b). The SAC is a five-item self-assessment. Participants are asked to rate themselves on such creativity-related questions as I consider myself to be very creative and I am good at coming up with new and different ideas. These items were modified from a study by J. C. Kaufman and Baer (2004b), which used personality-style items from the International Personality Item Pool (IPIP; Goldberg, 1999; Goldberg et al., 2006). Past studies

have shown that the SAC measure is correlated with both other self-report creativity measures (Wigert, Reiter-Palmon, Kaufman, & Silvia, 2012) and actual creative performance (J. C. Kaufman, Pumaccahua, & Holt, 2013; Wigert et al., 2012). In the current study, Cronbach's alpha coefficient for our sample of college students was r .91.

The study was performed in a quiet one-on-one setting. First, participants were administered the Atlantis and Rebus subtests. Next, they were administered the KTEA-II Brief Reading test, the two creative task prompts (poem and drawing), and a packet containing the Creative Achievement Questionnaire and the Self-Assessment of Creativity. This second part took 25 to 45 minutes to complete, providing the time gap needed for the third part, the delayed subtests, Atlantis Delayed and Rebus Delayed. All questionnaires and tests were given in random order within each section.

Coefficient alpha reliability analyses were first conducted for both CAT tasks, a recommended technique (Fleiss, 1981; Landis & Koch, 1977). Next, coefficients of correlation were computed among all intelligence and creativity tasks; because of the large number of coefficients computed, the alpha level was set at .01 to reduce the likelihood of interpreting chance findings as significant. Then four hierarchical linear regression analysis were conducted in two ways: (a) first, the various measures of creativity (the two rated prompts in the first block, followed by all 10 CAQ subtests, and SAC questionnaire in the second block) were used to predict performance on overall Glr and Gc; and (b) the intelligence measures (the overall Glr score in the first block and Gc in the second block) were used to predict two separate creativity outcomes—rated creativity in both Drawing and Poetry. The two actual creative products were selected because most of the debate over domain-specificity or domain-generality has emphasized the creative product as being a source of differences, as opposed to self-ratings or checklists (e.g., J. C. Kaufman & Baer, 2004a; Plucker & Beghetto, 2004).
The coefficient alpha reliabilities were r .83 for the poems (with six raters) and r .88 for the drawings (with seven raters).

Coefficient correlations above r = .75 are considered to be "excellent" (Fleiss, 1981).

Means and standard deviations were calculated for all intelligence subtests (see Table 1) and all creativity measures (see Table 2). For the individual intelligence subtests, the highest mean was for Atlantic Delayed at M = 9.22 and the lowest was for the Rebus Delayed at M = 8.07. For the CAQ, participants had the highest achievement in humor with an M = 1.02, and the lowest in architectural design with an M = 0.15.

Three sets of correlations were calculated: one with all the intelligence measures (see Table 3), one with all the creativity measures (see Table 4), and one with the intelligence by creativity measures (see Table 5). For the intelligence correlations, all coefficients were significant at the .01 level except Gc and Atlantis-Delayed. For the creativity subtests, the two CAT measures (Drawing and Poem) correlated significantly (r = .32) with each other. In general, however, most coefficients among the various measures of creativity were small and nonsignificant, ranging from -0.19 to .39. Table 5 reveals that rated creativity in drawing correlated significantly with both Glr and Gc, although the other correlations were typically nonsignificant and of trivial magnitude.

Hypothesis 1: The first two hierarchical multiple regressions used Glr and Gc as outcomes, with the two rated creativity measures in the first block and the rest of the creative measures in the second block. For Glr 15% of the variance was accounted for based on the Adjusted R-Squared by three predictors: Rated creativity in drawing (\beta = 0.35, t = 3.72, p < .001), self-reported music achievements (\beta = 0.22, t = 0.001)

2.12, p < .05), and self-reported theater and film achievements (\beta = 0.22, t = 2.19, p < .05). The model was significant at F(13, 101) = 2.53, p < .05. For Gc, 5% of the variance was accounted for based on the Adjusted R-Squared by Rated creativity in Drawing (\beta = 0.208, t = 2.17, p < .05). Model two was not significant and no additional predictors came out besides drawing so we retained the first model. The model was significant at F(2, 112) = 4.04, p < .005 (see Table 6).

Hypothesis 2: When we looked at rated creativity in drawing as an outcome with Glr in block one and Gc in block two, 13% of the variance was accounted for based on the Adjusted R-Squared by one predictor: Glr (\beta = 0.371, t = 4.26, p < .001). The overall model was significant at F(2, 113) = 10.33, p < .001. No models or predictors were significant when looking at rated creativity in poetry as an outcome variable (see Table 7).

The creativity measures accounted for a significant and notable percentage of the variance in Glr (15%) and a lower (but still significant) percentage of the variance for Gc (5%), supporting the first hypothesis. In addition, Glr accounted for 13% of the variance in the rated creative drawing task, whereas neither Glr nor Gc accounted for a significant percentage of the variance for the rated creative poetry task, supporting the second hypothesis.

There are a few notable findings to discuss. First, this study is the first to examine how Glr is related to actual creative performance as assessed by the Consensual Assessment Technique. Given both the CHC theory's prominence in the intelligence research literature and the extensive empirical investigations of creativity's relationship to intelligence, these results are notable in and of themselves. Second, although the component of Glr that is primarily associated with creativity is fluency, this study shows that the other components of Glr are also related to creativity. These results support the combination of these elements into Glr in the CHC theory (McGrew, 2005).

Finally, the creative drawing-intelligence link is noteworthy as it is consistent with studies showing that human figure drawings made by children and adults (to the simple prompt, draw a man, draw a woman, or draw a child) correlate substantially with conventional measures of intelligence (Koppitz, 1968). Indeed, the Draw-A-Person test has long been considered to provide an adequate measure of intelligence, especially for individuals with lim-

The findings support a domain-specific perspective of creativity. According to the Amusement Park Theoretical Model of Creativity (Baer & Kaufman, 2005; Kaufman & Baer, 2005), creativity can be conceptualized as a hierarchical system ranging from general creativity to some very broad areas (such as visual arts) to more specific areas (such as abstract painting). One of the tenets of this model is that related constructs such as intelligence, motivation, and personality will relate differently to creativity depending on the domain in which creativity is expressed. This study found that creative drawing performance was strongly tied to intelligence,

Given that people with high Glr can retrieve information fluently from long-term memory, it is possible that a more traditional measure of creativity (such as divergent thinking) may have shown an even stronger association. A key ability used in divergent thinking is having high verbal or figural fluency (i.e., being able to come up with many different responses to open-ended stimuli). Glr may be a stronger predictor of other measures of creativity that rely on concepts such as fluency. Indeed, as Silvia et al. (2013) demonstrated, divergent thinking is related to fluency-based measures of Glr.

There are several limitations that we hope will be addressed and expanded on in future work. At the most basic level, the number of participants in this study was small compared with the number of predictors. Although the analyses conducted were chosen with the current sample size in mind, future studies would ideally include more participants. In addition, many different domains and methodologies of creativity could be studied. In addition, in this study the prompts for the drawing versus the poem may have inadvertently had an impact with a person's creativity. The drawing prompt (Draw something that makes you happy) may have conceivably triggered a good mood, and the writing prompt (Write a poem about an embarrassing moment) may have triggered a negative mood. Isen and her colleagues (Isen, Daubman, & Nowicki, 1987; Isen, Johnson, Mertz, & Robinson, 1985) conducted a series of studies in which they induced good mood then measured creativity; people in good moods tend to be more creative. However, the mood-creativity association is complex (e.g., Kaufmann & Vosburg, 1997, 2002) and mood induction is not a simple process; indeed the methods that traditionally lead to mood changes that impact creativity are different from a simple sentence (Baas, De Dreu, & Nijstad, 2008).

A future direction for work—and a limitation to the current study—is that additional CHC constructs (most notably, Gf) were not included. Given Gf's strong if inconsistent relationship with creativity (e.g., Nusbaum & Silvia, 2011), future work should look at how both constructs are related to creative performance. Other facets of the CHC model should also be included. For example, although much of the work on memory and creativity focuses on long term storage and retrieval, there have been studies that explore working memory's relationship with creativity. Takeuchi et al. (2011) looked at brain activity during working memory performance, and found that more creative people were more likely to
use the precuneus area, which associated with mind wandering. Short-term memory (Gsm) may therefore have an interaction with creative performance.

Martindale (1999) proposed that processing speed would be differentially related to creativity. He argued that more creative people would have slower processing speed early in creative performance, during the planning stage, but would then be faster in later stages of creative performance. Later empirical studies lent support for these ideas (Dorfman, Martindale, Gassimova, & Vartanian, 2008; Vartanian, Martindale, & Kwiatkowski, 2007). Given these findings, the CHC factor of Processing Speed (Gs) would be another relevant variable to study. Reading and Writing (Grw) also taps into skills that have been hypothesized to relate to creative performance (J. C. Kaufman et al., 2011). In this study, rated creative writing did not significantly relate to Glr; it likely would be associated with Grw.

Just as more intelligence factors could have measured, so too could more creativity domains been assessed. Other possible domains might include science, math, problem solving, social interaction, dramatic or musical performance, or business (Ivcevic, 2007; J. C. Kaufman, 2012; J. C. Kaufman et al., 2009). Ideally, a future investigation could look at multiple CHC factors and multiple domains of creativity. Nearly all of the investigations of creativity and intelligence have used basic measures of g and a general measure of creativity, divergent thinking (Kim, 2005). It is only in the last decade that modern theories of intelligence, such as CHC, have been considered; even then, however, studies have been primarily restricted to Gf and Gc. Based on past research, it seems that both divergent thinking and remote association measures of creativity reflect Gf, Gc, and Glr.

Future work could establish a structural model of domain-specific creative performance and how it relates to intelligence. For example, creative ability in the visual arts might be linked to Glr (as in our study) and, potentially, Gv (visual processing). Creativity in the verbal arts does not seem to be related to Glr based on the current study, but likely relates to Gf and Grw. It would be possible to hypothesize further based on the existing creativity-intelligence field; creativity in science would likely encompass Gf, Gc, and Glr (among others); creativity in mathematics would also likely include Gq (quantitative reasoning). Creativity in performance domains may be less related to intellectual abilities and more related to personality traits (e.g., Nettle, 2006).

Plucker and Renzulli (1999) called for research studying how creativity and intelligence are related (and not whether), yet the last 15 years have primarily produced studies that continue to rely on basic g and c measures of intelligence and creativity. Our study provided evidence that both Glr and multiple domains of creativity should be included in future work. We hope that the nuances and intricacies of these complex constructs will continue to be examined closely.

Members of Underrepresented Groups: Reviewers for Journal Manuscripts Wanted

If you are interested in reviewing manuscripts for APA journals, the APA Publications and Communications Board would like to invite your participation. Manuscript reviewers are vital to the publications process. As a reviewer, you would gain valuable experience in publishing. The P&C Board is particularly interested in encouraging members of underrepresented groups to participate more in this process.
If you are interested in reviewing manuscripts, please write APA Journals at Reviewers@apa.org. Please note the following important points:
• To be selected as a reviewer, you must have published articles in peer-reviewed journals. The experience of publishing provides a reviewer with the basis for preparing a thorough, objective review.

• To be selected, it is critical to be a regular reader of the five to six empirical journals that are most central to the area or journal for which you would like to review. Current knowledge of recently published research provides a reviewer with the knowledge base to evaluate a new submission within the context of existing research.

• To select the appropriate reviewers for each manuscript, the editor needs detailed information. Please include with your letter your vita. In the letter, please identify which APA journal(s) you are interested in, and describe your area of expertise. Be as specific as possible. For example, "social psychology" is not sufficient—you would need to specify "social cognition" or "attitude change" as well.
• Reviewing a manuscript takes time (1– 4 hours per manuscript reviewed). If you are selected to review a manuscript, be prepared to invest the necessary time to evaluate the manuscript thoroughly.

APA now has an online video course that provides guidance in reviewing manuscripts. To learn more about the course and to access the video, visit http://www.apa.org/pubs/authors/reviewmanuscript-ce-video.aspx.
